title: Turbans, not helmets
hookLine: Sikh soldiers kept their turbans instead of steel helmets

cards: Two things on a table. One is a steel helmet, round and heavy, the kind armies issued in that war against flying metal. The other is a long strip of cloth, folded, waiting to be tied.
Every morning in the trenches, a Sikh soldier picked up the cloth. When the helmets came, the soldiers were asked to wear them.
The accounts from the war say Sikh soldiers kept their turbans and went into the line without the steel. Why would a man choose cloth over steel, where flying metal could kill him?
The answer starts with the hair underneath.

teach.h: KESH: UNCUT HAIR, ONE OF THE FIVE.
teach.b: First, the hair. Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five articles a Khalsa Sikh keeps, along with the comb, the steel bracelet, the short sword and the cotton undergarment.
The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks Sikhs to keep their hair uncut, as it grew. Second, the turban.

teach.h: THE DASTAR KEEPS IT. NOT A HAT.
teach.b: The dastar covers and keeps that hair. The code asks Sikh men to wear one, and some Sikh women wear one too. It isn't a hat; a hat comes off at the door.
The turban is part of how a Sikh keeps the Guru's form, and it is spoken of as a crown.

teach.h: A HELMET WOULDN'T SIT ON IT.
teach.b: Third, the helmet. A steel helmet would not sit over a turban, and taking the turban off to fit one would mean setting aside what the code asks a Sikh to wear over uncut hair.
So the accounts say the soldiers kept their turbans, and took the danger that came with that. Fourth, what it says today.
A turban can be seen from across a street.

It tells everyone who you are before you speak, which is a kind of courage on an ordinary Tuesday, in an office, on a bus, at a school gate. The soldiers wore it into the trenches. Sikhs today tie it before work.

how: Sikhs who keep their hair uncut tie the dastar each morning; Sikh men wear it as the Rehat Maryada asks, and some Sikh women wear one as well.

games.why: the accounts say Sikh soldiers kept their turbans and took the danger that came with it. the turban stayed.

practice: Sit tall, as if something you value were resting on your head.

If you wear a turban, a kara, a cross, a scarf or a ring that means something, feel its weight and where it touches you; if not, think of one thing people can see about you that you'd keep even when it costs you, an accent, a name, a habit of kindness.
Breathe in and own it, breathe out and let the worry about other people's eyes loosen, and if you pray, Waheguru fits here too.

wordCard.voice: Turbans. The dastar, the cloth that covers and keeps a Sikh's uncut hair, which Sikh soldiers kept on when the steel helmets came. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the turban stayed. Cloth kept on, where steel was offered. Day nine hundred ninety-eight, done.
